This section describes the raw data sources and the preparation pipeline that
turns them into the analysis-ready datasets used throughout the report.

## Data Sources

Four raw datasets underpin the analysis: taxi trip records, hourly weather
observations, points of interest, and a boundary layer of Chicago's community
areas. Each is described below by origin, coverage, and native granularity;
the cleaning and feature-engineering steps applied to each follow in the next
four subsections.

The taxi trip records come from the Chicago Data Portal's Taxi Trips dataset.
Before import, the file was already filtered to drop trips missing a pickup or
dropoff census tract and trips with zero recorded seconds or miles, and
trimmed to sixteen fields: trip and taxi identifiers, start and end
timestamps, trip duration and distance, pickup and dropoff census tract and
community area codes, the fare total, the operating company, and pickup and
dropoff coordinates. What remains is 6,041,177 trips spanning January 2024
through April 2026, each one a dispatched, metered ride at whatever time and
location a passenger requested it, which is the pattern the client's own
fleet will eventually have to anticipate.

Weather observations come from the ERA5-Land reanalysis product, pulled
through the Copernicus Climate Data Store API for a single coordinate near
Chicago (latitude 42, longitude -87.8) rather than a network of ground
stations. The record runs from January 1, 2024 through May 12, 2026 at hourly
resolution and carries six variables: 2-metre air temperature, total
precipitation, snow cover, snow depth, and the two horizontal components of
wind at 10 metres. A reanalysis is a modeled reconstruction rather than a
direct station reading, but it gives complete, gap-free hourly coverage for
the entire trip period, which no single Chicago weather station could
promise.

Points of interest come from OpenStreetMap, extracted with OSMnx for the
"Chicago, Illinois, USA" boundary and limited to three tag families: amenity,
shop, and tourism. The raw download returns 43,237 points spread across 311
distinct combinations of those tags, later collapsed into fourteen categories
relevant to travel demand (food and drink, nightlife, entertainment, and so
on) during preparation. Unlike the trip and weather data, this is a snapshot
of the map as it stands today, not a historical record tied to the trip
period.

The fourth source is a boundary layer for Chicago's 77 official community
areas, used for spatial reference and choropleth mapping throughout the
report. It is a distinct unit from the census tracts already present in the
trip data itself: the taxi records carry pickup and dropoff census tract and
community area codes directly, sourced under the portal's own privacy rules,
while this boundary layer only supplies the outlines needed to draw them on a
map.

## Points of Interest

<!-- Source notebook: notebooks/1.3 POIDataPrep.ipynb -->

Point-of-interest data was optional under the assignment brief, but
urban-analytics research treats POI density as one of the more reliable
proxies for where and when ride demand originates: restaurants and nightlife
venues draw evening trips, transit hubs and offices draw commute-time trips,
and the mix varies enough by neighborhood to be worth capturing alongside the
taxi and weather data.

We extracted points of interest from OpenStreetMap using OSMnx, querying the
"Chicago, Illinois, USA" boundary for three tag families: amenity, shop, and
tourism. The query returned 43,237 points, and coverage across the three tags
is uneven: 7,053 records lack an amenity tag, 37,552 lack a shop tag, and
41,738 lack a tourism tag, so most points carry only one of the three. We
combined the three columns into a single poi_type field by taking amenity
where present and falling back to shop, then tourism; every point ended up
with one of 311 distinct raw types, and none were left without a type or
without geometry.

At 311 distinct raw types, the data is too granular to use directly as model
features, so we imposed a manual mapping from each raw type to one of
fourteen broader categories that plausibly drive ride-hailing demand: food
and drink, nightlife, entertainment, leisure and sports, grocery, shopping,
health, finance, education, lodging, transport, automotive, services, and
civic and community. The mapping doubles as a filter. Fifty-five raw types,
mostly infrastructure and hyper-local street furniture such as benches,
parking entrances, post boxes, waste bins, and device charging stations, do
not fit any category and were dropped into an "other" bucket rather than kept
as noise. That bucket absorbs 23,129 of the 43,237 points, leaving 20,108
categorized points of interest.

Each retained point was assigned to an H3 hexagon at both resolution 7 and
resolution 8 from its centroid coordinates, then aggregated to the hexagon
level: a count of points, a count of distinct POI types, and the categorized
counts in wide format with one column per category. At resolution 7, 152
hexagons contain at least one point of interest; at resolution 8, that rises
to 806 hexagons, since the finer grid packs the same points into a larger
number of smaller cells. These per-hexagon POI counts and category breakdowns
feed directly into the feature set used for demand prediction in
@sec-prediction.
